title: The silk-cotton tree
hook: the silk-cotton tree is tall and straight, but its fruit is tasteless and its leaves useless (Asa di Var, ang 470)

segments.voice: Yesterday, mitthat neevee: on the scale, the side that bends low is heavy. Today we go back to the start of that salok, where Guru Nanak points at a tree.

In parts of North India and Punjab, there's a tree that's hard to miss when it blooms. Its branches are bare, and then suddenly they're covered in huge red flowers, so bright they look painted on. It stands tall and straight, often taller than everything around it. In Punjabi it's the simmal. In English, the silk-cotton tree, for the fluffy cotton in its pods. People in Guru Nanak's world knew it well, and he used it to open yesterday's salok, as a picture of a certain kind of life.
screen: `RED FLOWERS ON BARE BRANCHES.` → `TALL AND STRAIGHT.` → `THE SIMMAL TREE.`

segments.voice: Here's the salok's opening on ang 470, in paraphrase. The simmal tree is straight as an arrow, very tall and very thick. But the birds that come to it full of hope go away disappointed. Its fruits are tasteless, its flowers sickly, and its leaves are of no use. That's the whole picture, and it's sharp. From a distance, the tree has everything: height, straightness, a trunk you can't get your arms around, a blaze of color. A bird flying over would think: there's my meal, there's my shade. It lands, and finds nothing to eat, no shade worth sitting in. The tree isn't wicked. It just isn't useful. Right after the tree come the lines we heard yesterday: mitthat neevee are the essence of virtue; the side of the scale that bends low is the heavy one. So the tree is the opposite of the scale. All height and no weight. All show and no fruit. The salok keeps going, too. It describes the guilty one who bows twice as low, the way a hunter crouches to stalk a deer. Low, but not humble. Then it asks: what's the use of bowing the head if the heart stays impure? Put together, the lesson is about what people come to us for. Someone in trouble doesn't need us to be impressive. They need fruit: a meal, a kind word, real shade. The salok measures a life by what it gives, not how tall it stands.
screen: `TALL, STRAIGHT, THICK, BRIGHT.` · `THE BIRDS LEAVE DISAPPOINTED.` · `ALL HEIGHT, NO WEIGHT.` · `PEOPLE NEED FRUIT, NOT HEIGHT.` · then, large: `USEFUL, NOT TALL.`

segments.voice: Picture the people who might come to you this week hoping for something, a coworker, a child, a neighbor, and ask what fruit each would actually need: time, help, a listening ear, not a performance. Choose one small fruit you could give, and hold that picture for a few breaths. If you pray, say Waheguru.
Simmal, the silk-cotton tree: tall, straight and bright, but the birds that come to it in hope leave with nothing.
Your line: useful, not tall. Fruit feeds; height only looks good. Day five hundred fifty-two, done.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear the salok of the simmal tree in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and teachers use it to describe a life that looks impressive but gives nothing.

original.note: Gurmukhi: simmal, the silk-cotton tree, tall and red-flowered, common across Punjab.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty tree in an old poem.
what it means: a life that looks tall and impressive but gives nothing to those who come in hope.
what a scholar hears: the simmal opens the same salok as mitthat neevee; tree and scale are a pair, all height set against true weight.

chat.says: Why does Guru Nanak pick on a tall tree with beautiful flowers?
options: Because birds come in hope and leave hungry: it's all height and no fruit, show without giving.
Because tall trees are proud, and he teaches that every beautiful thing in the world is wicked.
Because its flowers are poisonous, so the salok warns people never to go near it at all.
chat.meaning: The simmal is straight, tall and bright, but its fruit is tasteless. The salok measures a life by what it gives, not how tall it stands.

simmal.meaning: the silk-cotton tree, tall and red-flowered

Punjab.meaning: the land of five rivers, where the Sikh faith began

sources.ref: Asa di Var, salok M1 (simmal rukh saraaiaa), Ang 470

notes: The salok is paraphrased; confirm the tree description (saraaiaa, ati deeragh, ati much), birds coming in hope and leaving disappointed, fruit tasteless (phikke), flowers sickly (bakbake), leaves useless.
The hunter line ('apraadhee doonaa nivai jo hantaa miragaahi') rendered as a hunter crouching to stalk a deer; confirm.
Botany: the simmal (Bombax ceiba, red silk-cotton) flowers on bare branches in late winter to early spring; confirm phrasing.

Fresh review: hook's seasonal claim softened and 'something we've all met... in ourselves' cut; the hunter line now names the guilty one (apraadhee) as the salok does; the closing claim narrowed from Sikh teaching as a whole to the salok. Day 551 no longer teaches the bowing warning, so it is fresh here.
